text.p: Hebron, where an Israeli soldier opened fire on Arabs on Wednesday, is a town divided. Here are some facts about it:

LOCATION: Situated in hills 30 km (18 miles) south of Jerusalem, Hebron is the last of seven Israeli-occupied West Bank towns due to be given Palestinian rule under a September 1995 peace deal. It is the only one of the seven where Jews live in the heart of an Arab population and the only one where the handover to self-rule has yet to be implemented.

RELIGIOUS IMPORTANCE: The Tomb of the Patriarchs, holy to Jews and Moslems, is the traditional burial place of the Bible's Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and their wives Sarah, Rebecca and Leah. Moslems know the tomb as al-Ibrahimi mosque.
NAME: The name Hebron derives from the Hebrew word "haver", or friend. In Arabic, the town is known as al-Khalil, meaning "the beloved", as in the beloved Abraham.
POPULATION: Some 100,000 Arabs and 400 Jewish settlers, including Jewish religious seminary students, live in the town.

THE DIVISION: Under the self-rule deal, 80 percent of Hebron will be turned over to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's police. The remainder, under Israeli army control, includes the Jews, 15,000 to 20,000 Arabs, and the Tomb of the Patriarchs. Joint patrols will act where necessary for security.
MODERN HISTORY: Arab rioters opposed to the growing number of Jewish immigrants in British-mandated Palestine massacred 67 Jews in Hebron in August 1929.
The town was under Jordanian rule from 1948, the year Britain left, until 1967 when Israel captured it with the rest of the West Bank in war.

In 1968, Jews led by Rabbi Moshe Levinger returned, renting a small hotel and announcing they would resettle the town. After three weeks the group moved to Hebron military headquarters where they lived until the founding of the adjacent Kiryat Arba Jewish settlement in 1971, which has since grown to 6,000 people. Jews resettled the heart of Hebron in 1979.
In February 1994, Kiryat Arba settler Baruch Goldstein massacred 29 Palestinians kneeling in prayer at al-Ibrahimi mosque in the Tomb of the Patriarchs before survivors beat him to death.

FUTURE OF JEWISH SETTLEMENTS: The fate of the Jews in Hebron and in other West Bank settlements is supposed to be decided in "final-status" talks between Israel and the Palestinians due to be completed by May 1999. Right-wing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed never to uproot the Jews of Hebron. Critics brand settlements a provocation and obstacle to peace. Some Israelis argue a military force should not be tied down protecting Hebron's Jews.
